title: European Commission outlines practical steps for implementing new EU rules on driving licences and driving disqualifications
source_name: 欧盟委员会交通与运输总司
content: The European Commission has published its implementation strategy for its Directives to modernise EU rules on driving licences and driving disqualifications. These initiatives aim to increase road safety across the EU, reducing the number of road deaths as well as undue administrative burden on citizens and authorities. With today’s implementation strategy, the Commission strives to support Member States in implementing these new EU rules, which include measures such as the introduction of an EU-wide accompanied driving scheme for 17-year-old drivers, a probationary period for novice drivers, as well as more systematic checks of peoples’ fitness to drive. In addition, the new rules adjust training and testing requirements to place greater emphasis on the safety of vulnerable road users, such as pedestrians, cyclists and micromobility users. The implementation strategy also sets out key steps for the introduction of mobile EU driving licences, as well as the EU-wide recognition of driving disqualifications, which ensures that drivers who commit serious traffic offences are held accountable whether they drive in their own country or elsewhere in the EU. The Commission aims to support Member States through a structured implementation approach based on different guidance documents, technical exchanges, cross-border cooperation projects, implementing and delegated acts, templates, peer learning and risk-based monitoring. Background Road safety is a major societal issue. In 2025, an estimated 19,400 people were killed on EU roads. The EU has set itself the ambitious target of ‘Vision Zero’ – zero road deaths by 2050, with an intermediate target of reducing fatalities by 50% by 2030. Road safety is a shared responsibility between the EU and Member States. While national and local authorities deliver most day-to-day actions, the EU contributes with safety rules for infrastructure and vehicles and for driver testing and licencing, coordinates cross-border cooperation between authorities and efforts to exchange best practices, and funds road safety projects. title: Solidarity Lanes: stronger cooperation to safeguard Ukraine’s access to world markets
source_name: 欧盟委员会交通与运输总司
content: Today, high-level representatives from Ukraine, Romania, Moldova and the European Commission discussed security threats to commercial navigation in the Black Sea and the Danube, following the intensification of unjustified attacks on civilian ships by Russian forces. The meeting took place as part of the ongoing implementation of the Solidarity Lanes Action Plan. It confirmed that the four parties – together known as the ‘Quad’ – remain very much committed to supporting Ukraine’s access to world markets through enhanced cooperation along the Danube corridor. The Quad firmly condemned Russia’s attacks against ships and port infrastructure, which has caused the disruption of traffic in Black Sea ports, and puts at risk the freedom of navigation in the Black Sea. All four parties stand ready to implement additional, alternative routes to limit the impacts on Ukraine’s exports and imports. Today’s meeting was held in the context of the Solidarity Lanes, a cooperative initiative that has established new transport routes for Ukraine’s exports and imports. To date, the Solidarity Lanes have helped Ukraine export around 226 million tonnes of goods, such as grain, ore and steel, and import around 108 million tonnes of essential merchandise, including fuel, vehicles, fertiliser as well as military and humanitarian assistance. The Solidarity Lanes pass through the Danube region, Poland, the Baltics, and the Adriatic region, via rail, road and inland waterways.
